name: Electric Charge & Conservation
short_explanation: Charge is an intrinsic property of matter (positive or negative). Like charges repel, opposite charges attract, and total charge is conserved (Q = ne).

name: Conductors and Insulators
short_explanation: Conductors contain abundant free electrons that readily migrate, whereas insulators hold electrons tightly in chemical bonds.

name: Electrostatic Force
short_explanation: The electrostatic force between two static charges is directly proportional to the product of charges and inversely proportional to the square of the separation distance.

name: Electric Current Definition
short_explanation: Electric current is the net rate of flow of electric charge across a cross-section: I = Q / t, measured in Amperes (A = C/s).

name: Electric Circuit & Continuity
short_explanation: A continuous and closed conducting loop through which electric current can flow between power terminals.

name: Ammeter Measurement
short_explanation: An ammeter measures electric current and must always be connected in SERIES. It possesses near-zero internal resistance to avoid reducing loop current.

name: Drift Velocity & Electron Flow
short_explanation: Electrons drift very slowly (mm/s) toward positive terminal, while the electric field establishes nearly at the speed of light throughout the conductor.

name: Electric Potential
short_explanation: Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing it from infinity to that point in an electric field.

name: Potential Difference (Voltage)
short_explanation: The work done to move a unit positive charge between two points: V = W / Q, measured in Volts (1 V = 1 Joule / Coulomb).

name: Voltmeter Connection
short_explanation: A voltmeter measures potential difference across two points and must be connected in PARALLEL. It has exceptionally high resistance so minimal current passes through it.

name: Chemical Cell & EMF
short_explanation: A cell maintains continuous potential difference across its terminals by converting chemical energy into electrical energy, driving charge movement.

name: Ohm's Law
short_explanation: At constant temperature, current flowing through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends: V = IR.

name: V-I Graph & Characteristics
short_explanation: For an ohmic conductor, the V vs I plot is a straight line through the origin. The slope of V vs I equals resistance R.

name: Electrical Resistance
short_explanation: The opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of electric charges due to frequent collisions between drifting electrons and positive metal ions.

name: Geometric Factors of Resistance
short_explanation: Resistance R is directly proportional to length L and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area A: R = ρ (L / A).

name: Resistivity (Specific Resistance)
short_explanation: Resistivity (ρ) is an intrinsic material property independent of dimensions, representing resistance of a 1 m cube. Measured in Ohm-meters (Ω·m).

name: Temperature Effect on Resistance
short_explanation: For pure metals, resistance increases with temperature as ionic lattice vibrations intensify, creating more electron scattering.

name: Series Combination: Current
short_explanation: In a series circuit, there is only a single path: the current through every component is strictly identical (I = I1 = I2 = ...).

name: Series Equivalent Resistance
short_explanation: Total equivalent resistance in series is the algebraic sum: Rs = R1 + R2 + ... + Rn. It is always greater than the largest individual resistance.

name: Parallel Combination: Voltage
short_explanation: In parallel combination, all components share the same two junction nodes, meaning potential difference across each branch is identical (V = V1 = V2 = ...).

name: Parallel Equivalent Resistance
short_explanation: Reciprocal of equivalent resistance is the sum of reciprocals: 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... Total resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance.

name: Series vs Parallel Dynamics
short_explanation: Parallel circuits allow independent appliance control without voltage drop. Series circuits fail completely if any single component breaks.

name: Joule's Law of Heating
short_explanation: Heat produced in a resistor is proportional to square of current, resistance, and time: H = I^2 R t = V I t = (V^2 / R) t.

name: Heating Effect Applications
short_explanation: Employed in electric heaters, toasters (nichrome wire with high resistivity and melting point) and tungsten filaments in incandescent bulbs.

name: Commercial Unit of Energy (kWh)
short_explanation: The commercial electrical energy unit is kilowatt-hour (kWh), commonly known as a 'unit'. 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10^6 Joules.

name: Electric Power Formulas
short_explanation: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed: P = V × I = I^2 R = V^2 / R, measured in Watts (W = J/s).

name: Appliance Ratings & Brightness
short_explanation: A bulb marked (100 W, 220 V) has fixed resistance R = V_rated^2 / P_rated. Its actual brightness depends on actual power consumed under the circuit's current or voltage.

name: Electric Fuse Safety
short_explanation: A safety device with a low melting point conductor connected in series with the live wire. Excessive current causes Joule heating to melt the fuse wire, breaking the circuit.

name: Domestic Circuits & Earthing
short_explanation: Household circuits run appliances in parallel at 220 V. Earthing provides a zero-resistance safe path to ground during insulation breakdown, preventing lethal shocks.
